newsitem.title: USA: US traders see surge in European gasoline imports.
newsitem.headline: US traders see surge in European gasoline imports.

text.p: U.S. traders Tuesday said they expect sharply nigher gasoline imports from Europe beginning next week, offsetting domestic production lost from Gulf Coast refinery turnarounds and ongoing repairs to a giant New Jersey catalytic cracker.

"There's a significant amount of European imports coming from January 20th to the end of the month," said one international trader, who estimated gasoline and blendstocks will average about 350,000 barrels per day (bpd) during the 12-day period.

That is almost three times more than usual, based upon U.S. Department of Energy data showing a daily average of about 80,000 barrels of European gasoline and 47,000 barrels of European blendstocks arriving during the first nine months of 1996.

"You can expect about 15-20 cargoes by the end of January," the trader said, with the arbitrage window for European imports remaining faintly open Tuesday as U.S. spot prices hovered about five cents a gallon higher than the European material.

One player said several of the European cargoes "will almost certainly" end up in Florida and other Southeastern U.S. ports because differentials on conventional unleaded gasoline on the East Coast and Gulf Coast are only one cent apart - an unusual phenomenon.

Gulf Coast diffs are usually at least about two cents a gallon weaker than East Coast prices -- allowing for the cost of transporting the fuel from Refinery Row in Texas and Louisiana to the Southeast.

But ongoing Gulf Coast refinery maintenance turnarounds have propped up Gulf diffs, traders said, making it cheaper for Southeastern buyers to purchase their supplies from Europe rather than from Gulf Coast producers.
"There's quite a lot of European product coming in - lots of it," another trader said.
But he predicted prices would remain stable because of the Gulf turnarounds and the temporary loss of the giant 140,000 bpd catalytic cracker at Tosco Corp's Bayway refinery in New Jersey.
The cracker is believed to have been taken out of action about a week ago for repairs and maintenance, with return to service not expected for at least two more weeks.
Other traders said the European imports will also offset a recent decline in imports of refined products from Venezuela, which averaged about 62,000 bpd during the first nine months of 1996.
A steady stream of European cargoes will continue arriving well into February, European traders said Tuesday, with over a dozen ships already fixed for liftings in the second half of this month.
The typical transatlantic journey time is estimated by shipbrokers at around two weeks.
((- Ransdell Pierson, New York Energy Desk, 212 859-1632))
